newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds buoyed by mild inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds buoyed by mild inflation data.

text.p: The Dow industrials Tuesday soared to its 40th record close this year and long-term bond interest rates slid close to 6 percent on fresh signs that inflation is in check.
The dollar fell against a strengthening British pound but rose against the German mark and Japanese yen despite new complaints from U.S. businesses that a strong U.S. currency will hurt the economy.
The blue-chip Dow ended up 50.69 points at 6,397.60, setting its ninth record out of the past 10 trading sessions, and beating Friday's high of 6,348.03.
It slipped 1 point Monday after rallying more than 350 points in the previous two weeks.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,435 to 1,008 on active volume of 454 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"What a great tape. Oh my God! It's the most powerful bull market of all time and has the horses to go higher," said James Cramer of Cramer Co.
"The true leadership is Microsoft, Intel and IBM," he said. "It feels like '85 and '86. The market wants to go somewhere and it has to travel a lot of points to get there."

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 5.14 to 742.16, topping the old record close of 737.62 set Friday. The NYSE Composite gained 1.90 to 391.80, also topping Friday's record 390.02.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond rose 14/32, or $4.375 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield down to 6.44 percent from 6.47 percent at Monday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Bonds rose after October housing starts fell 5.1 percent to an annualized 1.366 million rate, the lowest since October 1995.
The data provided further proof that the economy is slowing and there is no reason to worry that the Federal Reserve will need to raise interest rates to slow growth.
"The bond's going to 6 percent, so you're not making money there," Cramer said.
"The consumer domestic economy is slowing down. But the corporate domestic economy is fine and and the international corporate economy is also doing well," he said.
But Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James, remains cautious. "IBM is like the market. It's standing on a stilt. We're in an acceleration phase, a straight up move."
The dollar rose to 111.65 yen from 111.53 yen late Monday and climbed to 1.5055 marks from 1.5020 marks.
The pound rose to a fresh four-year high of $1.6769 on Tuesday and set a 30-month high against the mark. It fetched $1.6755 in late trading, up from $1.6710 late Monday.
Heating oil prices rallied in New York as demand was seen increasing on forecasts of subnormal temperatures in the U.S. Northeast and Midwest at a time when inventories are low.
Heating oil for December delivery finished 1.83 cents higher at 73.68 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Heating oil's rally paced gains in the rest of the oil complex, with December crude ending up 61 cents at $24.49 a barrel, and December gasoline settling 1.62 cents higher at 67.39 cents a gallon.
December gas oil, the European equivalent of heating oil, ended $3.00 a metric ton higher at $221.50 on reports of snow in Europe.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index closed at 3,978.1, up 16 points on the day. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average gained 159.81 points to close at 20,956.18.
